lessons.title: What an LLM actually does
lessons.summary: A large language model predicts likely next words from patterns in its training data. That single fact explains most of its strengths and failures.

sections.heading: Prediction, not lookup
sections.body:
A large language model (LLM) such as the GPT models behind ChatGPT is trained on huge amounts of text to predict what text should come next. It doesn't look facts up in a database by default; it generates text that **fits the patterns** it learned.

That's why it is excellent at drafting, rephrasing, summarising and explaining, and why it can produce fluent text that is wrong.

sections.heading: Tokens and the context window
sections.body:
Models read and write in **tokens** (chunks of words). Everything the model can "see" in a conversation (your messages, uploaded files, its own replies, instructions) has to fit in its **context window**.

- Very long chats or huge files can push early details out of view or dilute attention.
- When a long conversation starts drifting, start a fresh chat with a short summary of what matters.

sections.heading: Knowledge cutoff and tools
sections.body:
A model's built-in knowledge stops at its **training cutoff**. Without tools, answers draw only on that training data. For anything recent (prices, news, policies, product versions) use ChatGPT's **search** or **deep research**, connect a relevant **app**, or give it the source document yourself.

When ChatGPT uses search, it shows sources. Open them: a citation shows where a claim came from, not that the claim is right.

sections.heading: Same prompt, different answers
sections.body:
Generation involves **sampling**: at each step the model picks from several likely next tokens rather than always the single top one. So the same prompt can give different wording, a different structure or even a different conclusion.

- Variation is expected behaviour, not a fault, and it doesn't mean either answer is a hallucination.
- Treat the first answer as a draft. For decisions, regenerate or ask again in a fresh chat, compare the runs, and ask for reasoning, alternatives and sources.
- Points that recur across runs are more stable; points that appear once deserve extra checking. Agreement between runs is still **not** proof: verify facts against a source.
- When you need consistent output (for example a recurring report), reduce the freedom: give a fixed format, an example and the source material.

keyPoints: LLMs generate likely text; they are not databases of facts.
Everything in the chat must fit in the context window; long chats degrade.
Built-in knowledge has a cutoff; use search, deep research or your own documents for current facts.
Outputs vary between runs: treat answers as drafts.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a confident, well-written answer is accurate.
gotchas.correct: Fluency is not accuracy. Verify facts, figures and quotes, especially ones you will publish or act on.

gotchas.trap: Asking about last month’s news without turning on search.
gotchas.correct: Use search or deep research, or paste the source, for anything after the model’s cutoff.

lessons.lab: Ask ChatGPT the same question three times in three new chats: "What are the three biggest risks for a mid-size retailer adopting AI?" Compare the answers. Which points repeat? Which appear only once? Write one sentence on what that tells you about trusting a single answer.

lessons.title: Hallucinations and other failure modes
lessons.summary: Know the ways ChatGPT goes wrong so you can catch them before they reach a customer or a decision.

sections.heading: Hallucination
sections.body:
A **hallucination** is confident, plausible content that is false: an invented statistic, a quote nobody said, a court case that doesn't exist, a wrong product feature.

Risk is highest for **specific details**: names, numbers, dates, citations, legal or medical specifics, and niche topics with little training data.

sections.heading: Confidence isn't reliability
sections.body:
OpenAI's own help center warns that ChatGPT can be wrong while sounding certain, and that **confidence isn't reliability**. Hallucinations include fabricated quotes, studies, citations and references to sources that don't exist.

- Use ChatGPT as a **first draft, not a final source**.
- Always verify quotes, data, technical information and references to external documents.
- Even when an answer includes citations, **open the links yourself** and check they say what is claimed.
- Asking the model "Are you sure?" is not verification: it can confirm its own error just as fluently.

sections.heading: Other common failures
sections.body:
- **Sycophancy:** agreeing with you because you sounded sure. Ask it to argue the other side.
- **Over-generalising:** turning one example into a rule.
- **Missing context:** it can't know your company's policies, numbers or customers unless you provide them.
- **Arithmetic and counting slips** in plain text: ask it to use data analysis (it runs code) for calculations.
- **Bias** inherited from training data, in wording, examples or assumptions about people.

sections.heading: Reducing the risk
sections.body:
- Give it the source material and tell it to answer **only from the provided documents**, saying "not in the source" when something is missing.
- Ask for **quotes or page references** for key claims.
- For numbers, upload the data and have it compute with data analysis rather than estimate.
- Allow uncertainty: "If you are not sure, say so."

sections.heading: Things it can't reliably do
sections.body:
- **Detect AI-written text.** ChatGPT cannot reliably tell whether a piece of text was written by AI, so don't use it to judge a student's essay or a job applicant's cover letter.
- **Know your private context.** It doesn't know internal data, policies or customers unless you provide or connect them.
- **Know recent events** without search or a source you supply.

keyPoints: Hallucinations cluster in specifics: numbers, names, dates, citations.
Grounding answers in provided documents and asking for quotes reduces risk.
Use data analysis (code) for calculations, not mental arithmetic.
Invite disagreement to counter sycophancy.
Confidence isn't reliability: use output as a first draft, not a final source.
ChatGPT cannot reliably detect AI-written text; don't use it as a detector.

gotchas.trap: Asking ChatGPT "Are you sure?" and accepting "Yes" as verification.
gotchas.correct: Self-confirmation is not verification. Check the claim against a primary source.

gotchas.trap: Letting it total a long column of numbers in plain chat.
gotchas.correct: Upload the file and ask it to calculate with data analysis, then spot-check the result.

gotchas.trap: Pasting an essay and asking ChatGPT whether AI wrote it, then acting on the answer.
gotchas.correct: ChatGPT can't reliably detect AI-generated text. Use your organisation's process and evidence, not a model's verdict.

lessons.lab: Paste a one-page document and ask: "Answer only from this document. Quote the sentence that supports each answer. If the document doesn't say, reply 'not in the source'." Then ask two questions the document does answer and one it doesn't. Did it hold the line on the third?

lessons.title: Anatomy of a good work prompt
lessons.summary: Most weak output comes from weak briefs. Brief ChatGPT like a smart new colleague who knows nothing about your situation: say what you want, what it needs to know, what the result should look like and what must not change.

sections.heading: The four parts (plus optional extras)
sections.body:
OpenAI's current prompting guide names four parts of a work prompt:

1. **Goal:** what you want done. Start with the result you want rather than a list of steps.
2. **Context:** the information or sources that help: background, audience, what already exists, files to use.
3. **Output:** the format, length and level of detail: a table, 150 words, three bullets, headings.
4. **Boundaries:** what must stay unchanged or what needs your approval first. Focus on the one or two boundaries that matter most.

Two optional extras often help as well:

- **Role or perspective:** "Review this as a skeptical CFO would."
- **Examples:** a sample of the style or format you want (see the next lesson).

You don't need every part every time. A short prompt is often enough; for larger or more important tasks, include the parts that matter.

sections.heading: Boundaries: what must not change
sections.body:
Boundaries are the part people most often forget. They tell ChatGPT where it must not go:

- "Don't change the figures in the table, only the commentary."
- "Keep the legal disclaimer word for word."
- "Suggest edits, but check with me before rewriting the conclusion."

Pick the one or two that really matter. A long list of minor rules dilutes the ones that protect you.

sections.heading: Before and after
sections.body:
Weak:

```
Write an email about the new expense policy.
```

Strong:

```
You're writing to 40 field sales reps who submit expenses from their phones.
Goal: get them to use the new expense app from 1 March; old forms will be rejected.
Write a friendly email under 150 words with: a one-line summary, 3 bullet steps
to get started, the deadline in bold, and who to contact (finance-help@).
Avoid jargon and don't mention the old vendor.
```

sections.heading: Structure long prompts
sections.body:
For longer briefs, separate parts with headings or tags so instructions don't blur into source material:

```
## Instructions
Summarise the customer interviews below for the product team.
## Output
Top 5 themes, each with a supporting quote and how many interviews mentioned it.
## Interviews
[paste here]
```

sections.heading: Say what to do, not only what not to do
sections.body: "Write in short, plain sentences for a general audience" works better than a list of prohibitions. Positive instructions give the model a target.

keyPoints: OpenAI's guide: Goal, Context, Output, Boundaries.
Start with the result you want, not a list of steps.
Boundaries say what must stay unchanged or needs your approval; keep to the one or two that matter.
A short prompt is often enough; add parts as the stakes and size grow.
Name the audience and purpose, and specify length and structure.
Separate instructions from pasted material with headings.
Positive instructions beat lists of don'ts.

gotchas.trap: One-line prompts for important deliverables.
gotchas.correct: Spend a minute on context, output and boundaries. It saves several rounds of rework.

gotchas.trap: "Make it better."
gotchas.correct: Say what better means: shorter, more formal, for executives, with numbers, fewer bullets.

gotchas.trap: Writing a long, every-part prompt for a quick everyday question.
gotchas.correct: A short prompt is often enough. Scale the brief to the size and importance of the task.

gotchas.trap: Saying "tidy up this report" and getting changed numbers back.
gotchas.correct: State the boundary: "Edit wording only; don't change any figures."

gotchas.trap: Claiming OpenAI teaches a fixed six-part framework.
gotchas.correct: OpenAI's guide names four parts (Goal, Context, Output, Boundaries); role and examples are useful optional extras.

lessons.lab: Take a real task from this week. Write the prompt you'd normally use, run it, then rewrite it with a clear goal, the context it needs, the output you want and one or two boundaries, and run that. Compare the two outputs and note how many edits each would need.

lessons.title: Examples, iteration and breaking work down
lessons.summary: Show what you want, iterate in small steps, and split big jobs into stages you can check.

sections.heading: Show, don’t only tell
sections.body: Paste one or two **examples** of the style or format you want ("Here are two past newsletters we liked"). Models imitate examples closely, so pick good ones and vary them if you don't want everything to look identical.

sections.heading: Iterate like an editor
sections.body:
The first prompt doesn't need to be perfect. **Iterate rather than restart:** review the result, then

- ask for the specific change: "Keep sections 1 and 3, rewrite 2 for a non-technical reader."
- add a missing source: "Here is the Q3 forecast; update the numbers paragraph to use it."
- correct the direction: "This should persuade, not inform. Lead with the cost saving."
- ask for another option: "Give me three alternative subject lines, more urgent."

If a chat goes badly off track after many turns, start a new chat with a clean, complete brief that includes your corrections.

sections.heading: Decompose big tasks
sections.body:
For a large deliverable, go in stages and check each one:

1. Outline → you approve.
2. Draft each section → you review.
3. Tighten and format.

Stages catch wrong directions early and keep each request focused.

sections.heading: Ask it to ask you
sections.body: When you're not sure what context matters: "Before you start, ask me up to five questions you need answered to do this well."

sections.heading: Finish with a check
sections.body: For important work, ask ChatGPT for a **final check** ("Check this against the brief and list anything missing or inconsistent"), then **review the result yourself** before you use or share it. The model's check helps; it doesn't replace yours.

sections.heading: Refine recurring prompts before you automate them
sections.body: If a prompt will run every week (a status summary, a news digest), get it right in a **normal chat** first. Run it, fix what's wrong, and only then schedule it (for example as a Scheduled Task). Automating an untested prompt just repeats its flaws on a timer.

keyPoints: The first prompt doesn't need to be perfect; iterate rather than restart.
Give targeted edits: the specific change, a missing source, a new direction or another option.
One or two good examples shape style and format strongly.
Split big work into outline, draft and polish stages.
Let ChatGPT interview you for missing context.
For important work, ask for a final check, then review it yourself.
Refine a recurring prompt in a normal chat before scheduling it.

gotchas.trap: Asking for a 20-page report in one prompt.
gotchas.correct: Outline first, then draft section by section, checking as you go.

gotchas.trap: Correcting the same mistake again and again in a long, messy chat.
gotchas.correct: Start a fresh chat with a complete brief that includes the correction.

gotchas.trap: Scheduling a weekly report prompt you have never run by hand.
gotchas.correct: Refine it in a normal chat until the output is right, then schedule it.

gotchas.trap: Treating ChatGPT's own "final check" as sign-off.
gotchas.correct: Use its check as a prompt for your review, then review the result yourself before sharing.

lessons.lab: Ask ChatGPT to interview you ("ask me 5 questions first") before drafting a one-page project update. Then produce it in two stages: outline, then full draft. Note which of its questions surfaced context you would have left out.

lessons.title: Prompt patterns for everyday tasks
lessons.summary: Reusable patterns for summarising, drafting in your voice, analysing, brainstorming and preparing for meetings, the everyday tasks OpenAI's AI Foundations course applies prompting to.

sections.heading: Summarise for a purpose
sections.body:
```
Summarise this 30-page vendor proposal for our COO, who has 2 minutes.
Give: price and term, the 3 biggest risks to us, anything that differs from
our RFP requirements, and a one-line recommendation. Quote clause numbers.
```

sections.heading: Draft in your voice
sections.body:
Paste two or three of your own past messages and say "Match the tone and sentence length of these." Add what the draft must say and who it's for, because examples set style, not facts.

For a voice you use every day, save tone preferences in **custom instructions** (which apply to all chats) or in a **project's instructions** (which apply only inside that project). Then read the draft as yourself: would you actually send it?

sections.heading: Analyse and decide
sections.body: Ask for **options with trade-offs**, not one answer: "Give three ways to reduce onboarding time, each with cost, effort, risk and what we'd need to believe for it to work."

sections.heading: Brainstorm widely, then narrow
sections.body: Ask for many ideas fast ("20 webinar titles"), then a second step to score them against your criteria. Separating generation from judgment gives better variety.

sections.heading: Meeting prep
sections.body:
Give it the inputs you'd read yourself and ask for what you need walking in:

```
Here are the agenda and last meeting's notes. List the decisions we need,
likely objections from finance, and three questions I should ask.
Keep it to one page.
```

Afterwards, paste your notes and ask for a summary of decisions, owners and deadlines. Check names, dates and commitments against what was actually said.

keyPoints: Summaries should name the reader and what they need to decide.
Voice drafting: paste your own samples for style, and supply the facts separately.
Ask for options with trade-offs, not a single answer.
Generate broadly first, then evaluate in a separate step.
Meeting prep: give agenda and notes; ask for decisions, objections and questions.
Store recurring tone and context in custom instructions or a project.

gotchas.trap: "Summarise this" with no audience or purpose.
gotchas.correct: Say who will read it, how long they have and what they need to decide.

gotchas.trap: "Write this in my voice" with no samples of your writing.
gotchas.correct: Paste a few real examples of your messages; the model can't guess your style.

gotchas.trap: Sending a meeting summary without checking owners and dates.
gotchas.correct: Verify names, dates and commitments against your notes before circulating.

lessons.lab: Build a personal prompt library: write one reusable prompt each for summarising, drafting an email, comparing options and meeting prep. Save them where you can reuse them (for example in a project's instructions or a notes doc).

lessons.title: Verifying facts, numbers and sources
lessons.summary: A practical routine for checking ChatGPT output before you use it, scaled to the stakes.

sections.heading: Scale checking to the stakes
sections.body:
- **Low stakes** (brainstorm, internal first draft): skim for sense.
- **Medium** (internal decisions, team docs): check key facts and numbers.
- **High** (customers, executives, legal, medical, financial, public): verify every claim against a **primary source** and have a qualified person review.

sections.heading: The checking routine
sections.body:
1. **Highlight checkable claims:** numbers, names, dates, quotes, "studies show".
2. **Open the sources** ChatGPT cites. Confirm the source exists, is credible and actually says that.
3. **Recompute numbers** from the data, or have data analysis show its working, then spot-check.
4. **Check against your own knowledge** and internal systems of record.
5. **Look for what's missing:** risks, counterarguments, affected groups.

sections.heading: Ask for evidence up front
sections.body: "For each claim, give the source and a direct quote." "Separate what the document says from your own inferences." These make checking faster and expose weak claims.

sections.heading: First draft, not final source
sections.body: OpenAI's help center advises using ChatGPT "as a first draft, not a final source" and to always verify quotes, data, technical information and references. A confident tone tells you nothing: **confidence isn't reliability**. Even when an answer has citations, open the links yourself.

keyPoints: Match verification effort to how the output will be used.
Open cited sources and confirm they say what is claimed.
Recompute or spot-check every number that matters.
Ask for quotes and a split between facts and inferences.
High-stakes content needs a qualified human reviewer.
Treat output as a first draft; a confident tone is not evidence.

gotchas.trap: Treating a link in the answer as proof.
gotchas.correct: Open it. Sources can be misread, outdated, low quality or not say what the answer claims.

gotchas.trap: Sending AI-written numbers to a client unchecked.
gotchas.correct: Recompute from the source data before anything leaves the team.

gotchas.trap: Asking ChatGPT "Are you sure?" and accepting a yes.
gotchas.correct: Self-confirmation is not evidence. Check the claim against a primary source.

lessons.lab: Ask ChatGPT with search for "5 statistics about remote work productivity with sources". Check each one: does the source exist, is it credible, does it say exactly that, and how old is it? Score how many survive.

lessons.title: Critiquing and improving drafts
lessons.summary: Use ChatGPT as an editor and reviewer, with clear criteria, while keeping your own judgment in charge.

sections.heading: Review against criteria
sections.body: Give explicit criteria: "Review this proposal as a skeptical procurement lead. Score clarity, evidence, risks addressed and call to action from 1–5, explain each score, then list the three changes that would raise the scores most."

sections.heading: Fresh eyes beat self-review
sections.body: A model asked to review what it just wrote, in the same chat, tends to defend it: the conversation already frames the draft as its answer. For a more honest critique, paste the draft into a **new chat** (or give it to a colleague) together with the review criteria. This is common course guidance rather than a documented product rule, so treat it as a habit, not a guarantee.

sections.heading: Check for bias and gaps
sections.body: Ask: "Who might be left out or treated unfairly by this text? What assumptions does it make about the reader?" Review job ads, policies and customer messages for exclusionary wording.

sections.heading: Know when to stop
sections.body: Endless polishing has diminishing returns. Decide upfront what "good enough" means for this use (the audience, the must-haves, the risks that must be covered), check the draft against that bar, and ship. If each new round only swaps synonyms or reshuffles sentences, you are past the bar. If a round keeps surfacing *new factual problems*, stop prompting and go back to the sources.

keyPoints: Critiques are better with explicit criteria and a reviewer persona.
Review in a fresh chat to avoid the model defending its own draft.
Ask directly about bias, exclusion and hidden assumptions.
Define "good enough" before you start polishing.

gotchas.trap: Asking the same chat that wrote the draft to grade it.
gotchas.correct: Use a fresh chat or another reviewer with clear criteria.

gotchas.trap: Polishing until ChatGPT stops suggesting changes.
gotchas.correct: It will always find something. Stop when the draft meets the bar you set for its purpose.

lessons.lab: Write (or have ChatGPT write) a short job ad. In a new chat, ask for a review for clarity, inclusive language and unnecessary requirements. Apply the changes you agree with and note any you rejected and why.

lessons.title: Building review into your workflow
lessons.summary: Turn checking from an afterthought into planned steps: a final check you then review yourself, verifiable research, checked numbers and human checkpoints in repeatable work.

sections.heading: Ask for a final check, then review it yourself
sections.body:
OpenAI's prompting guide says that for important work you should **ask for a final check, then review the result yourself** before using or sharing it. The model's check is a useful first pass: it can catch inconsistencies, missing sections or claims that don't match an attached file. It does not replace your review, because you are accountable for what you send.

A useful final-check prompt names what to look for: "Check this against the brief: list any requirement not met, any number that doesn't match the attached data, and any claim with no source."

sections.heading: Make research verifiable from the start
sections.body: Deep research produces cited, structured reports. You can **edit the research plan** before it starts, watch progress and interrupt it, and **limit research to specific sites or trusted apps**. Use those controls so the sources are ones you would accept, then still open the citations that support the claims you rely on. Citations make checking faster; they don't do it for you.

sections.heading: Check numbers where they are made
sections.body: When data analysis computes figures from a spreadsheet, ask it to show the steps or code it ran and the rows it included. Then spot-check a few figures by hand or in your own spreadsheet, and confirm totals reconcile with your system of record. Watch for silently dropped rows, wrong date ranges and mixed units.

sections.heading: Put checkpoints into repeatable work
sections.body: OpenAI Academy's Applied AI Foundations course has learners plan workflows in terms of **inputs, models, tools, checkpoints and human review**. Decide where a person must look before work moves on: before anything goes to a customer, before a number reaches a decision, before an action can't be undone. Refine a recurring prompt in normal chat, checking its output, before you schedule it.

sections.heading: What ChatGPT can't check for you
sections.body: ChatGPT cannot reliably tell whether text was written by AI, so don't use it as an AI-text detector. It also can't confirm facts it has no access to, such as internal decisions or data you haven't shared. Those checks need people and systems of record.

keyPoints: For important work: ask for a final check, then review it yourself.
Shape deep research up front (plan, trusted sites), then open the key citations.
Ask data analysis to show its working, then spot-check and reconcile totals.
Plan checkpoints and human review into repeatable workflows.
ChatGPT is not a reliable AI-text detector.

gotchas.trap: Treating the model's own final check as the review.
gotchas.correct: It is a first pass. You still review the result before using or sharing it.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a deep research report is verified because it has many citations.
gotchas.correct: Open the citations behind the claims you will rely on and confirm they say that.

gotchas.trap: Scheduling a recurring prompt before its output has been checked.
gotchas.correct: Refine and check it in normal chat first, then schedule it, with a human checkpoint where it matters.

lessons.lab: Upload a small spreadsheet and ask data analysis for three summary figures. Ask it to show the steps it ran. Recompute one figure yourself, then ask for a final check of the summary against the data. Note anything the model's check missed that your own check found.

lessons.title: Choosing the right ChatGPT tool and reasoning level
lessons.summary: ChatGPT is a set of tools: Chat for quick help, Work for longer multi-step deliverables, plus search, deep research, data analysis and images. Pick the tool and the reasoning level to fit the task.

sections.heading: The toolkit (names and plan availability change: check the current help center)
sections.body:
- **Chat:** fast, conversational help for everyday questions, drafting, rewriting and brainstorming. Longer writing and code now happen directly in the chat as writing blocks and code blocks.
- **Search:** recent or real-time information with cited sources.
- **Deep research:** multi-step research across many sources that returns a structured, cited report. It takes longer than a quick search. You can edit the research plan before it starts, watch and interrupt progress, and limit it to specific sites or trusted apps.
- **File uploads and data analysis:** read documents; analyse spreadsheets and CSVs by running code; produce charts and files.
- **Image input and generation:** describe or analyse uploaded images, and generate or edit visuals such as mock-ups and diagrams.
- **Voice:** talk through ideas hands-free.
- **ChatGPT Work:** an agent for longer, multi-step work and finished deliverables (research, analysis, documents, spreadsheets, presentations, reports). It gathers information across your files and connected apps and checks in for approval before important actions.

sections.heading: What changed recently
sections.body:
ChatGPT changes quickly, so learn the job each tool does rather than its name.

- The older **ChatGPT agent** (agent mode) is no longer available; longer multi-step tasks now go to **ChatGPT Work**.
- **Canvas** was removed from current models; writing and code happen in chat through writing and code blocks.
- **Codex** sits alongside Chat and Work and is aimed at software development.

sections.heading: Match the task
sections.body:
| Task | Best fit |
|---|---|
| Draft a reply or rewrite a paragraph | Chat |
| What changed in a regulation this year | Search, or deep research for a full cited report |
| Analyse six months of sales data and chart it | Data analysis on the uploaded file |
| Make a mock-up image for a slide | Image generation |
| Pull data from several files and apps into a finished report or deck | ChatGPT Work |
| Compare 15 vendors' public pricing pages | Deep research or Work, then review the result |

sections.heading: Models and reasoning
sections.body: The model picker offers a fast option (**Instant**) and higher **reasoning levels** that spend more time working through a problem before answering. Use the fast option for simple, everyday tasks such as rewording, short drafts and quick questions. Use a higher reasoning level for complex analysis, multi-step planning, maths and tricky trade-offs where accuracy matters more than speed. More reasoning is slower and isn't automatically better for simple tasks, and it never removes the need to check the result. Model names and which levels each plan gets change often, so learn the trade-off rather than the names.

keyPoints: Chat is for quick help; ChatGPT Work is for longer, multi-step work that ends in a finished deliverable.
Search and deep research are for current or sourced information; deep research plans can be edited and limited to specific sites.
Data analysis runs code on your files: use it for calculations and charts.
Image generation creates and edits visuals; it doesn't analyse data.
Use the fast option for simple tasks and a higher reasoning level for complex, multi-step or high-stakes analysis.
Canvas and the old ChatGPT agent have been retired; don't plan workflows around them.

gotchas.trap: Using plain chat without search to answer questions about this week's events.
gotchas.correct: Use search, or deep research for a full cited report.

gotchas.trap: Using deep research for a quick factual lookup.
gotchas.correct: Deep research is a longer multi-step process; use search for quick lookups.

gotchas.trap: Setting the highest reasoning level for every message.
gotchas.correct: Match the level to the task: fast for simple edits, higher reasoning for complex multi-step problems.

gotchas.trap: Looking for agent mode or canvas to run a multi-step task.
gotchas.correct: Those were retired. Use ChatGPT Work for multi-step deliverables and chat writing blocks for long drafts.

lessons.lab: Do one small task each with search, data analysis (upload a CSV) and image generation. Then run one multi-step analysis twice, once with the fast option and once with a higher reasoning level, and write one line on whether the extra time was worth it.

lessons.title: Projects, memory, plugins and apps
lessons.summary: Stop re-explaining context: organise recurring work with custom instructions, memory, projects, and plugins that connect ChatGPT to your tools.

sections.heading: Custom instructions and memory
sections.body:
**Custom instructions** tell ChatGPT about you and how you like answers (role, tone, format) and apply to all your chats. **Memory** lets ChatGPT use useful details across chats. In Settings > Personalization you can review and delete what it remembers, control whether it references saved memories and chat history, or turn memory off. Deleting a chat doesn't necessarily delete a memory saved from it, so remove the memory itself if needed.

A **temporary chat** doesn't create or update memories and doesn't appear in your history. Use it when you don't want a conversation to shape future answers.

sections.heading: Projects
sections.body: A **project** groups related chats, files and instructions in one place: a client, a product launch, a recurring report. **Project instructions apply only inside that project and override your global custom instructions.** Projects can use **project-only memory** so context from one piece of work doesn't leak into unrelated chats; shared projects always use project-only memory. Projects can be shared with collaborators (check current plan availability and file limits).

sections.heading: Plugins and apps
sections.body: An **app** connects ChatGPT to an external service such as email, a calendar, a drive or a work system, so it can search and use that data. A **plugin** packages capabilities into a workflow and can include apps, skills or both; you find them in the Plugin Directory. (Apps used to be called connectors.) Access follows your permissions in those tools, and each app has a permission setting, from always asking before an action to allowing all actions. Workspace admins control which apps and plugins are available.

sections.heading: Custom GPTs are being replaced
sections.body: **Custom GPTs are being retired and migrated to plugins.** In the migration, a GPT's instructions become a skill, its knowledge files become reference files and its connected apps carry over. Some settings, such as custom actions, model selection and sharing settings, don't migrate, so recheck them. Don't start new repeatable workflows as custom GPTs; check the help center for current dates.

sections.heading: Choosing between them
sections.body:
- A preference that applies everywhere → custom instructions.
- An ongoing piece of work with files and its own rules → project (with project-only memory if it must stay separate).
- A repeatable workflow with skills and connected tools → plugin.
- Needs live company data → an app connection, if your admin allows it.
- A one-off sensitive conversation that shouldn't be remembered → temporary chat.

keyPoints: Custom instructions apply to all chats; project instructions override them inside a project.
Memory is viewable and controllable; deleting a chat doesn't necessarily delete a saved memory.
Project-only memory keeps context from one piece of work separate from others.
Apps connect ChatGPT to external services; plugins bundle apps and skills into workflows.
Custom GPTs are being retired and migrated to plugins.
Temporary chats don't appear in history or create memories.

gotchas.trap: Pasting the same background into every new chat.
gotchas.correct: Put it in a project's instructions and files, or in custom instructions.

gotchas.trap: Building a new custom GPT for a team's repeatable workflow.
gotchas.correct: Custom GPTs are retiring. Use a shared project or a plugin instead.

gotchas.trap: Deleting a chat and assuming everything it taught ChatGPT is gone.
gotchas.correct: Check and delete the saved memory itself, or use a temporary chat next time.

gotchas.trap: Setting an app to allow all actions for convenience.
gotchas.correct: Pick the most restrictive permission that does the job, such as always asking before actions.

lessons.lab: Create a project for one recurring piece of work. Add two reference files and project instructions (audience, tone, format) that differ from your global custom instructions. Turn on project-only memory if you can. Run two requests in it and check that both follow the project instructions without you repeating them.

lessons.title: Agents: delegating multi-step work
lessons.summary: An agent such as ChatGPT Work plans and carries out multi-step tasks across apps and files. Delegate well-defined work, set boundaries, and keep humans at the checkpoints that matter.

sections.heading: What an agent is
sections.body:
An **agent** is an AI system that works toward a goal over several steps, deciding what to do next and using **tools** (search, files, connected apps, code) along the way.

In ChatGPT today, **Chat** is for fast, conversational help, while **ChatGPT Work** is the agent for longer, multi-step work and finished deliverables such as research, analysis, documents, spreadsheets and presentations. Work gathers information across apps and files and pauses for approval on important actions. **Deep research** is a narrower agent-style feature that runs multi-step research and returns a cited report.

> The older ChatGPT agent ("agent mode") is no longer available; the help center points to ChatGPT Work instead. Product names change often, so learn the concept rather than the label.

sections.heading: Good tasks to delegate
sections.body:
- **Clear goal and finish line:** "Compile a table of the 10 largest competitors' public pricing, with links."
- **Reviewable output:** a draft-quality result you will check before using.
- **Tolerable risk:** low impact if a step goes wrong, or an approval before anything consequential.
- **Multi-step:** gathering, combining and formatting across several sources. A one-line question belongs in Chat.

Poor fits: vague goals ("improve our marketing"), high-stakes or irreversible actions with no review, and decisions about people (hiring, credit, medical, legal) that need human judgment.

sections.heading: Briefing an agent
sections.body:
Give an agent the same parts you would give a capable colleague:

- **Goal:** what to produce and what "done" looks like.
- **Context:** the sources, files or apps to use, and any to avoid.
- **Output:** format, length and level of detail.
- **Boundaries:** what must not change, and what needs your approval first.

Focus on the one or two boundaries that matter most rather than a long list of rules.

sections.heading: Human checkpoints and accountability
sections.body:
Decide where a person approves: before purchases, before messages go to customers, before records change, before anything is published. ChatGPT Work lets you decide what it can access, when it checks in and when it needs approval, and it pauses for approval on important actions. Approvals happen through on-screen controls, not by voice.

Safeguards reduce risk but don't eliminate it; content the agent reads on the web or in files can try to steer it (prompt injection). **You remain accountable** for what an agent does on your behalf, and OpenAI's usage policies prohibit automating high-stakes decisions in sensitive areas without human review.

keyPoints: Agents pursue a goal over many steps using tools; ChatGPT Work is the current agent for multi-step deliverables.
Use Chat for quick questions and Work for longer tasks that produce a finished deliverable.
Delegate tasks with a clear goal, finish line, reviewable output and tolerable risk.
Brief with goal, context, output and boundaries, including when to stop and ask.
Put human approval before consequential or irreversible actions; you stay accountable.

gotchas.trap: Letting an agent send customer emails or make purchases with no review.
gotchas.correct: Require approval before consequential actions and review results.

gotchas.trap: Giving an agent a vague goal like "improve our marketing".
gotchas.correct: Define the deliverable, sources, boundaries and what done looks like.

gotchas.trap: Assuming built-in safeguards make an agent risk-free.
gotchas.correct: Safeguards reduce but don't eliminate risk; keep checkpoints and review output.

lessons.lab: Write an agent brief for a research task: goal, sources to use or avoid, output format, and the boundary where it must stop and ask you. Run it with deep research or ChatGPT Work (whichever your plan offers) and list which parts of the brief it followed and which it missed.

lessons.title: From prompts to repeatable workflows
lessons.summary: Turn a prompt that works into a workflow with defined inputs, tools, checkpoints and human review, then automate it with Scheduled Tasks once it is reliable.

sections.heading: Why workflows, not one-off prompts
sections.body: A good prompt you retype every week is fragile: the inputs drift, steps get skipped and nobody checks the same things twice. A **workflow** makes the work repeatable: the same inputs go through the same steps, with the same checks, to a predictable output.

sections.heading: The workflow plan
sections.body:
OpenAI Academy's Applied AI Foundations course has learners write a workflow plan that covers:

1. **Inputs:** what goes in (files, data, apps, a form) and where it comes from.
2. **Models:** what level of reasoning each step needs. Fast for simple steps, more reasoning for complex or high-stakes analysis.
3. **Tools:** search, data analysis, connected apps, files.
4. **Checkpoints:** where the output is checked before moving on.
5. **Human review:** who approves, and before which actions.

Weigh **quality, speed and cost** together. The cheapest, fastest setup isn't the right one if errors reach customers.

sections.heading: Refine first, then automate
sections.body:
Refine a recurring prompt in a normal chat until it reliably produces what you want, and only then schedule it. Automating an unproven prompt just repeats its mistakes on a timer.

A sensible path: single prompt, then a reusable setup (for example a **project** with instructions and files, or a **plugin** that packages a workflow), then an agent or scheduled workflow. Measure time saved and error rate at each step before scaling. (Custom GPTs are being retired and replaced by plugins, so don't build new workflows around them.)

sections.heading: Scheduled Tasks
sections.body:
In ChatGPT Work, **Scheduled Tasks** can run **once**, **on a schedule**, **on an event** (for example a webhook from email, chat or code tools) or to **monitor for changes**. When you share a task, each recipient gets their own copy; your chat history, local files and memories don't transfer with it.

Automation doesn't remove checkpoints. A scheduled task that drafts a weekly summary can still stop for approval before anything is sent outside the team.

keyPoints: A workflow plan covers inputs, models, tools, checkpoints and human review.
Weigh quality, speed and cost; don't optimise one at the expense of errors.
Refine a recurring prompt in a normal chat before scheduling it.
Scheduled Tasks run once, on a schedule, on an event, or to monitor for changes.
Shared tasks give each recipient a copy without your history, files or memories.
Automated workflows still need human review before consequential actions.

gotchas.trap: Scheduling a prompt that has only worked once.
gotchas.correct: Refine it in a normal chat until it's reliable, then schedule it.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a shared scheduled task carries your memories and files to colleagues.
gotchas.correct: Each recipient gets their own copy; history, local files and memories don't transfer.

gotchas.trap: Building a new team workflow on a custom GPT.
gotchas.correct: Custom GPTs are retiring; use projects or plugins instead.

lessons.lab: Pick a task you do every week. Write a one-page workflow plan with inputs, model/reasoning level, tools, checkpoints and the human review step. Run it manually three times in a normal chat, note what you had to fix, and only then decide whether it is ready to schedule.

lessons.title: Data, privacy and workspace controls
lessons.summary: Know what you can share, which ChatGPT plan your company approved, and the controls that protect data.

sections.heading: Follow your company policy first
sections.body: Use the ChatGPT workspace your organisation approved (for example a Business, Enterprise or Edu workspace) for work data, not a personal account. Your company's data classification rules decide what can go in. When in doubt, leave it out or ask.

sections.heading: What workspace plans add (check current terms)
sections.body:
Workspace plans (Business, Enterprise, Edu and the healthcare and teacher variants) are designed for organisational use. OpenAI's enterprise privacy page states:

- **No training by default:** "We do not train our models on your data by default." Information reached through apps in Business, Enterprise and Edu is also not used for training by default.
- **Ownership:** you own your inputs and outputs (where allowed by law).
- **Security:** encryption at rest and in transit, SOC 2 Type 2 audits, and SAML single sign-on.
- **Admin controls:** which apps are enabled, data retention (Enterprise and Edu), and audit logs through the Compliance API (Enterprise, Edu and Healthcare).

Plan line-ups and features change often, so check current plans before quoting specifics.

sections.heading: Personal accounts: know the defaults
sections.body:
On personal plans (Free, Go, Plus, Pro) your content can be used to improve models **by default**. You can switch off **"Improve the model for everyone"** in Data Controls; it applies to the whole account, and archiving a chat does not change it.

**Temporary Chat** is not used for training, does not appear in your history and does not create memories, though it may be kept for a limited period for safety review. It reduces footprint; it does not make a personal account an approved place for company data.

sections.heading: Minimise sensitive data
sections.body:
- Don't paste passwords, API keys or secrets, ever.
- Remove or mask personal data (names, IDs, health or financial details) unless your policy allows it and it's necessary.
- Prefer summaries or anonymised samples over full customer records.

sections.heading: Accountability and disclosure
sections.body:
You are responsible for anything you send, publish or decide using ChatGPT. "The AI wrote it" is not a defence for an error in a client email or report.

- Treat output as a first draft, not a final source: verify before it leaves your hands.
- A named person owns each deliverable and approves it.
- Follow your organisation's rules on disclosing AI assistance, and be transparent where it matters (customers, academic work, regulated content).
- Don't let readers believe a human expert or credentialed professional produced something they did not.

keyPoints: Use the company-approved workspace for work data.
Workspace plans: no training on business data by default, you own inputs and outputs, plus admin controls (SSO, apps, retention, audit logs).
Personal plans train by default; turn off "Improve the model for everyone" in Data Controls.
Temporary Chat: no training, no history, no memories; still not an approved home for company data.
Never paste secrets; minimise personal data.
You remain accountable; disclose AI use where policy requires.

gotchas.trap: Using a personal ChatGPT account for confidential client files because it is faster.
gotchas.correct: Use the approved workspace and follow data classification rules.

gotchas.trap: Pasting a full customer export to "clean it up".
gotchas.correct: Share only the fields needed, anonymised, in an approved workspace.

gotchas.trap: Assuming Temporary Chat in a personal account makes it fine to paste confidential client data.
gotchas.correct: Temporary Chat limits history, memory and training, but company policy still decides which tool may hold work data.

gotchas.trap: Sending an AI-drafted client report unchanged because "ChatGPT wrote it, not me".
gotchas.correct: You own what you send. Verify it, have the accountable owner approve it, and disclose AI use where policy requires.

lessons.lab: Find your organisation's AI use policy (or draft a one-page version for your team): which tools are approved, what data is allowed, what needs review, and how to disclose AI use. Check one of your recent chats against it.

lessons.title: Bias, fairness, IP and responsible habits
lessons.summary: Use ChatGPT in ways that are fair to people and respectful of others’ work, and keep human judgment where it belongs.

sections.heading: Bias and fairness
sections.body: Models can reflect biases in their training data. Be most careful when output affects people: hiring, performance reviews, lending, customer treatment. Don't use ChatGPT as the decision-maker in those areas. Review wording for stereotypes and test with varied examples.

sections.heading: Intellectual property and confidentiality
sections.body: Respect copyright, licences and confidentiality when you upload or reuse content. Check your company's rules before using generated images or text commercially, and don't present others' work as your own.

sections.heading: Over-reliance
sections.body: OpenAI's own guidance: "Use ChatGPT as a first draft, not a final source." Keep your own expertise sharp. Use ChatGPT to speed up work you understand, and be extra careful where you can't judge whether the answer is right: get an expert to review. Confident wording is not evidence of correctness.

sections.heading: Usage policy basics
sections.body:
OpenAI's usage policies say responsible use is shared, and that the policies are no substitute for legal requirements, professional duties or ethical obligations. Prohibited uses include:

- **Automating high-stakes decisions without human review** in sensitive areas such as employment, credit, insurance, legal, medical and essential government services.
- **Tailored advice that requires a licence** (for example legal or medical) without a licensed professional involved, or implying the AI holds professional credentials.
- Deceptive or fraudulent use.
- **Circumventing safeguards.**
- Building facial-recognition databases without consent, and inferring emotions in the workplace (limited exceptions).

Breaking the rules may mean losing access; enforcement decisions can be appealed. Your company may add stricter rules. When ChatGPT declines a request, rephrase only if your purpose is legitimate, and never try to trick it around safety rules. The policy is updated from time to time, so check the current version.

keyPoints: Don't let ChatGPT make decisions about people; keep a human reviewer and check for bias.
Usage policies prohibit automating high-stakes decisions without human review.
Licensed advice needs a licensed professional involved; never imply the AI holds credentials.
Respect copyright, licences and confidentiality.
First draft, not final source: be most careful where you can't judge correctness yourself.
Follow OpenAI usage policies and your company's stricter rules; never circumvent safeguards.

gotchas.trap: Ranking job candidates with ChatGPT and using the ranking as the decision.
gotchas.correct: Humans decide. Use AI for structure (interview guides, criteria) and review it for bias.

gotchas.trap: Publishing ChatGPT's tailored legal advice to customers as if a lawyer wrote it.
gotchas.correct: Involve a licensed professional and don't imply the AI holds professional credentials.

gotchas.trap: Feeding a competitor's copyrighted article into ChatGPT to "reword it so it's ours".
gotchas.correct: Rewording through AI doesn't remove IP concerns. Create original work and follow licence and company rules.

lessons.lab: Ask ChatGPT to write three short customer personas. Review them for stereotypes or assumptions. Rewrite the prompt to reduce them and compare.

flashcards.front: What does an LLM fundamentally do?
flashcards.back: Predicts likely next tokens based on patterns learned in training. It generates fitting text rather than looking facts up.
A chunk of text (part of a word, a word or punctuation) that models read and write. Context-window limits are measured in tokens.
Everything the model can consider at once: instructions, messages, files and its own replies. Very long chats can degrade attention to early details.
The date after which the model has no built-in knowledge. Use search, deep research or your own documents for later information.
Confident, plausible but false content: invented facts, numbers, quotes or citations.
Specific details (names, numbers, dates, citations), niche topics, and legal, medical or financial specifics.
The model agreeing with the user because they sounded confident. Counter it by asking for the opposing case.

flashcards.front: Why can the same prompt give different answers?
flashcards.back: Generation involves sampling, so wording and even conclusions can vary. Treat answers as drafts.
Upload the data and use data analysis, which runs code, then spot-check the result.

flashcards.front: Long chat drifting off track: what do you do?
flashcards.back: Start a new chat with a concise, complete brief or summary of what matters.

flashcards.front: "Confidence isn't reliability": what does it mean in practice?
flashcards.back: A fluent, certain-sounding answer can still be wrong. Judge output by checking it against sources, not by its tone.

flashcards.front: Can ChatGPT tell you whether a text was AI-generated?
flashcards.back: Not reliably. Don't use it as an AI-text detector or base decisions about people on its verdict.

flashcards.front: What role should ChatGPT output play in your work?
flashcards.back: A first draft, not a final source. Verify quotes, data, technical details and references before you use or share it.

flashcards.front: The answer includes citations. Is it verified?
flashcards.back: No. Open the links yourself: a citation shows where a claim came from, not that the source says it or that it is correct.

flashcards.front: Two runs of the same prompt disagree. What is a sensible next step?
flashcards.back: Compare them, ask for reasoning and sources, and verify the disputed point against a primary source. Agreement between runs is not proof either.

flashcards.front: What are the main remedies for the knowledge cutoff?
flashcards.back: Search, deep research, connected apps, or pasting/uploading the source document yourself.

flashcards.front: Four parts of a work prompt in OpenAI's prompting guide?
flashcards.back: Goal (what to do), Context (information or sources that help), Output (format, length, detail) and Boundaries (what must stay unchanged or needs your approval). Role and examples are optional extras.
Audience sets vocabulary, length, depth and tone. "For a new hire" and "for the CFO" need different answers.
Examples show the style and format you want; models imitate them closely, so pick good, varied ones.
Specific edits: shorter, more formal, add numbers, rewrite section 2 for non-experts, three alternatives.

flashcards.front: How to handle a big deliverable?
flashcards.back: Decompose into stages (outline, draft sections, polish) and check each stage.

flashcards.front: What does "ask me questions first" achieve?
flashcards.back: ChatGPT surfaces the context it needs, which you might have left out.
Saying what to do ("short plain sentences") works better than long lists of don’ts.

flashcards.front: How to separate instructions from pasted material?
flashcards.back: Use headings or tags such as ## Instructions and ## Source so they don’t blur together.
Generate many options first, then evaluate them against criteria in a separate step.
Ask for several options with trade-offs (cost, effort, risk, assumptions), not a single answer.
Reader, their time budget, what they need to decide, and required items (risks, numbers, references).

flashcards.front: What are Boundaries in a work prompt?
flashcards.back: What must stay unchanged or what needs your approval first, e.g. "Don't change the figures" or "Check with me before rewriting the conclusion."

flashcards.front: How many boundaries should you list?
flashcards.back: Focus on the one or two that matter most. A long list of minor rules dilutes the important ones.

flashcards.front: Does every prompt need all the parts?
flashcards.back: No. A short prompt is often enough; for larger or more important tasks, include the parts that matter.

flashcards.front: Start a prompt with steps or with the result?
flashcards.back: With the result you want. Describe the outcome rather than prescribing a list of steps.

flashcards.front: First draft isn't right. Restart or iterate?
flashcards.back: Iterate: ask for the specific change, add a missing source, correct the direction or request another option. Restart only when a long chat has drifted badly.
Ask it for a final check against the brief, then review the result yourself before using or sharing it.
Refine it in a normal chat until the output is right. Scheduling an untested prompt repeats its flaws.

flashcards.front: How to get a draft in your own voice?
flashcards.back: Paste a few samples of your own writing to set style, give the facts and audience separately, and save standing tone preferences in custom or project instructions.
Give the agenda and prior notes; ask for decisions needed, likely objections and questions to ask. Afterwards, summarise decisions, owners and deadlines, then check them.
Scale to stakes: skim low-stakes drafts; check key facts for internal use; verify everything and get expert review for external or regulated content.

flashcards.front: Does a citation prove a claim?
flashcards.back: No. Open it to confirm it exists, is credible, is current and actually says that.
The original source of a fact (the dataset, regulation, filing, study), not a summary of it.

flashcards.front: How to ask for checkable output?
flashcards.back: Request a source and direct quote for each claim, and a split between facts and inferences.

flashcards.front: Why review in a fresh chat?
flashcards.back: The same chat tends to defend its own draft. A fresh context with clear criteria usually gives a more candid critique (a habit, not a guarantee).

flashcards.front: What makes a useful critique prompt?
flashcards.back: A reviewer persona, explicit criteria, scores with reasons, and the top changes that would help most.
"Who might be excluded or treated unfairly by this text, and what assumptions does it make?"
When the output meets the "good enough" bar you defined for its use.

flashcards.front: Is "Are you sure?" a verification method?
flashcards.back: No. Self-confirmation isn’t evidence; check a primary source.

flashcards.front: What to look for besides errors?
flashcards.back: What’s missing: risks, counterarguments, affected groups, edge cases.

flashcards.front: OpenAI's advice for important work before sharing?
flashcards.back: Ask ChatGPT for a final check, then review the result yourself before using or sharing it.

flashcards.front: "First draft, not a final source" means?
flashcards.back: Treat ChatGPT output as a starting point and verify quotes, data, technical details and references before relying on them.

flashcards.front: Does a confident tone mean the answer is right?
flashcards.back: No. Confidence isn't reliability; the model can sound certain and still be wrong.

flashcards.front: How to make deep research easier to trust?
flashcards.back: Edit the research plan before it starts and limit it to specific sites or trusted apps, then open the key citations.

flashcards.front: How to check numbers from data analysis?
flashcards.back: Ask it to show the steps it ran and rows used, spot-check a few figures yourself and reconcile totals with the source.
Not reliably. Don't use it as an AI-text detector.

flashcards.front: Where do checkpoints belong in a repeatable workflow?
flashcards.back: Before output reaches a customer or decision, and before irreversible actions: plan inputs, models, tools, checkpoints and human review.
For current facts or when you need cited sources quickly.
A multi-step research tool that reads many sources and produces a structured, cited report; it takes longer than a quick search.

flashcards.front: What is data analysis in ChatGPT?
flashcards.back: ChatGPT runs code on uploaded files to calculate, clean data and make charts or files.
It was removed from current models. Longer writing and code now happen in chat through writing blocks and code blocks.

flashcards.front: Fast option (Instant) vs a higher reasoning level?
flashcards.back: Fast for simple everyday tasks; higher reasoning for complex analysis, multi-step planning and maths, at the cost of speed.
Standing preferences about you and how you want answers, applied to all chats (project instructions override them inside a project).
ChatGPT using useful details across chats. You can review, delete or turn it off in Personalization settings.
A chat that doesn’t appear in history and doesn’t create or update memories.
A workspace that groups related chats, files and instructions for ongoing work. It can use project-only memory and be shared with collaborators.

flashcards.front: What is happening to custom GPTs?
flashcards.back: They are being retired and migrated to plugins: instructions become a skill, knowledge files become reference files and connected apps carry over.

flashcards.front: What is an app (formerly a connector)?
flashcards.back: A connection to an external service such as email, calendar, a drive or a work system, so ChatGPT can use that data within your permissions and admin settings.
Project for an ongoing body of work with its files and instructions; plugin for a packaged, repeatable workflow built from skills and apps.

flashcards.front: Best tool to compare 15 vendors’ public pricing?
flashcards.back: Deep research or ChatGPT Work, then review the result and open the sources.
An agent for longer, multi-step work that ends in a finished deliverable (report, spreadsheet, presentation). It works across files and apps and asks for approval before important actions.
Chat: fast everyday help. Work: longer multi-step deliverables. Codex: software development.

flashcards.front: Which controls does deep research give you?
flashcards.back: You can edit the research plan before it starts, watch and interrupt progress, and limit it to specific sites or trusted apps.
An app connects ChatGPT to one external service. A plugin packages a workflow and can include apps, skills or both.
Project instructions apply only inside that project and override your global custom instructions there.
Keeping context from one project separate from your other chats, e.g. for different clients. Shared projects always use it.

flashcards.front: Does deleting a chat delete memories saved from it?
flashcards.back: Not necessarily. Review and delete the saved memory itself in settings.
To create or edit visuals such as mock-ups, illustrations and diagrams. It doesn't calculate or analyse data.

flashcards.front: Is a higher reasoning level always better?
flashcards.back: No. It's slower and adds little for simple tasks, and it doesn't remove the need to check the output.
A system that pursues a goal over multiple steps, choosing actions and using tools.

ChatGPT's agent for longer, multi-step work and finished deliverables. It works across apps and files and pauses for approval on important actions. (It replaced the retired ChatGPT agent / agent mode.)
Clear goal and finish line, draft-quality result you’ll review, low risk or a confirmation step.
Before purchases, external messages, record changes, publishing or anything irreversible.

flashcards.front: Who is accountable for an agent’s actions?
flashcards.back: The person or organisation who delegated the task.
Single prompt → reusable setup (project or plugin) → agent or scheduled workflow, measuring value at each step.

flashcards.front: What should an agent brief include?
flashcards.back: Goal, sources to use or avoid, constraints, output format, and when to stop and ask.

flashcards.front: Five parts of a workflow plan (Applied AI Foundations)?
flashcards.back: Inputs, models, tools, checkpoints and human review, weighing quality, speed and cost.

flashcards.front: Ways a Scheduled Task can be triggered?
flashcards.back: Once, on a schedule, on an event (e.g. a webhook), or to monitor for changes.

flashcards.front: What transfers when you share a scheduled task?
flashcards.back: The task itself: each recipient gets their own copy. Your chat history, local files and memories don't transfer.

flashcards.front: When should you schedule a recurring prompt?
flashcards.back: After you've refined it in a normal chat and it reliably produces what you want.
Chat for fast, conversational help and quick questions; Work for longer, multi-step tasks that produce a finished deliverable.

flashcards.front: Do agent safeguards remove all risk?
flashcards.back: No. Approvals and built-in safeguards (such as auto-review of important actions) reduce risk but don't eliminate it; keep checkpoints and review output.
The workspace your organisation approved (e.g. Business, Enterprise, Edu), never a personal account for company data.
OpenAI states: "We do not train our models on your data by default" for workspace plans such as Business, Enterprise and Edu (check current terms).
Examples: SAML SSO, user management, which apps are enabled, retention (Enterprise/Edu) and audit logs via the Compliance API.
Passwords, API keys and other secrets.
Minimise, mask or anonymise; include only what policy allows and the task needs.
Humans decide. Use AI for structure and drafts, and review for bias.
Respect copyright, licences and confidentiality; check commercial-use rules for generated content.
Follow organisational rules; be transparent where it matters (customers, academic, regulated content).
Examples: automating high-stakes decisions without human review, unlicensed tailored professional advice, deceptive or fraudulent use, circumventing safeguards. Companies may add stricter rules.
Accepting answers you can't judge. Treat ChatGPT as a first draft, not a final source, and get expert review outside your expertise.
Personal plans train by default; turn off "Improve the model for everyone" in Data Controls (account-wide) or use Temporary Chat.

flashcards.front: Who owns inputs and outputs in a workspace plan?
flashcards.back: You do (where allowed by law), per OpenAI's enterprise privacy commitments.
Not used for training, not shown in history, creates no memories; may be kept for a limited period for safety. Not a substitute for an approved workspace.
Automating high-stakes decisions in sensitive areas (employment, credit, insurance, legal, medical, essential government services) without human review is prohibited.
Tailored advice that needs a licence requires a licensed professional involved; never imply the AI holds professional credentials.

flashcards.front: Who is accountable for AI-assisted work?
flashcards.back: You, the person who sends, publishes or decides. Verify, have an owner approve, and disclose AI use where policy requires.

flashcards.front: What happens if you break the usage policies?
flashcards.back: You may lose access; enforcement decisions can be appealed.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how ChatGPT produces an answer?
options: It generates text that is statistically likely given its training and the conversation
It retrieves the single correct answer from a verified fact database
It copies the most relevant web page word for word
It runs a search engine query for every message by default

rationales: Correct: generation by prediction explains both fluency and errors.
There is no built-in verified fact database.
It generates new text rather than copying pages.
Search is a tool used when enabled or needed, not for every message.

Finance topics are allowed.

A specific statistic with a named study and year

General advice is lower risk.

questions.stem: After 90 messages, ChatGPT starts ignoring the brand guidelines the manager gave at the start of the chat. What is the best fix?

Switch to voice mode
Ask the same chat whether it remembers the guidelines
Start a new chat with a concise brief that includes the brand guidelines, or put them in a project

rationales: Shouting doesn’t fix diluted context.
Voice doesn’t change the context problem.
Its answer won’t restore attention to early content.

questions.stem: You run the same prompt twice and get different recommendations. What does this show?
options: Generation involves sampling, so answers vary and should be treated as drafts to evaluate
ChatGPT is broken and should be reported
The second answer is always the correct one
The first answer was a hallucination

rationales: Correct: variability is expected behaviour.
Variation is not a bug.
Order says nothing about correctness.

Context window overflow
Knowledge cutoff
Sycophancy: the model tends to agree with a confidently stated view

rationales: No images are involved.
One message doesn’t overflow context.
Cutoff concerns dates, not agreement.

Upload the data and have ChatGPT compute results with data analysis, then spot-check
Recompute or verify key figures against the source system before sharing

rationales: Mental-arithmetic style estimates are error-prone.
Adjectives don’t improve numerical accuracy.
Correct: code-based calculation is more reliable than generated arithmetic.
Correct: verification against the system of record catches errors.

questions.stem: A product manager asks ChatGPT for a go/no-go recommendation on a feature launch. In one chat it says "launch"; in a fresh chat with the identical prompt it says "delay". What is the best interpretation and next step?
options: The second chat is more reliable because it had no earlier context, so go with "delay"
Output varies because generation involves sampling; compare the reasoning in both, ask for the key assumptions and evidence, and make the decision on the checked facts
ChatGPT is malfunctioning, so the recommendation should be discarded and the issue reported
Keep regenerating until two answers in a row agree, then use that answer
questions.explanation: Different answers to the same prompt are normal because the model samples from likely tokens. The useful move is to treat both as drafts, surface the reasoning and assumptions, and decide on verified facts. Majority voting between runs is not verification.
rationales: A fresh chat is not inherently more accurate; it is just another sample.
Correct: variability is expected; evaluate the reasoning and verify the underlying facts.

questions.stem: An analyst uses ChatGPT every Monday to turn the same type of status notes into a summary, but the structure of the summary changes from week to week. What is the most effective fix?

Switch to a different chat each week so earlier weeks don't interfere
Specify a fixed output format with headings and an example summary, and supply the notes as the source each time
Accept the variation, because the model's output cannot be steered
questions.explanation: Because generation is sampled, an under-specified prompt leaves room for variation. A fixed format, an example and the source material narrow that room and make outputs more consistent. Vague pleas for consistency don't constrain the output.
rationales: A vague instruction doesn't define what "consistent" means.
A fresh chat doesn't remove sampling variation.
Correct: explicit format plus an example reduces run-to-run variation.
Output can be steered substantially with format, examples and context.

Don't: ChatGPT cannot reliably detect AI-generated text, so its verdicts are not a sound basis for decisions about people

Context size isn't the problem; the task itself is unreliable.
Web search doesn't make AI-text detection reliable.

Correct: verify quotes and numbers at the source before sharing.
Links do not guarantee the source exists or says what is claimed.

questions.stem: A paralegal asks ChatGPT for case law supporting an argument and receives five well-formatted case names with years and short summaries. The answer sounds certain. What is the best way to treat this output?

As ready to file, because the formatting matches real legal citations

Blaming a fictitious glitch is deceptive.

questions.stem: A colleague used ChatGPT to help draft a funding proposal. The funder's guidelines require disclosure of generative AI assistance. What should they do?
options: Skip disclosure because they edited the text
Disclose only if the funder asks directly
Rewrite it in a different tool so it no longer counts as ChatGPT
Disclose the AI assistance as the guidelines require and remain responsible for the content
questions.explanation: Where an organisation or recipient requires disclosure, follow that rule; editing the text doesn't remove the obligation. The author remains responsible for accuracy and originality either way.
rationales: Editing doesn't remove a disclosure requirement.
The rule applies whether or not anyone asks.
Switching tools is evasion, not compliance.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which two practices best keep accountability clear when a team adopts ChatGPT for customer-facing emails? (Select two.)
options: A named owner reviews and approves each AI-assisted email before it is sent
Let ChatGPT send emails directly so humans are not a bottleneck
Follow the company's rule on when and how to disclose AI assistance to customers
Sign emails as "the AI team" so no individual is responsible
questions.explanation: Accountability needs a person who reviews and owns each output, plus transparency where policy requires it. Removing human review or diffusing ownership weakens both.
rationales: Correct: human review and ownership.
Removes the review step that catches errors.
Correct: transparency per policy.
Diffuses accountability instead of keeping it clear.

questions.stem: A colleague pastes a competitor's published blog post into ChatGPT and asks it to "reword it enough that it's ours" for your website. What is the best response?
options: Fine, because AI-reworded text is automatically original
Fine, as long as you add a few sentences of your own
Don't do it: rewording someone else's work through AI doesn't remove IP concerns; create original content and follow licence and company rules
Fine, if you use a Temporary Chat so there is no record
questions.explanation: Respect copyright and don't present others' work as your own; routing it through a model doesn't change that. Hiding the activity in a Temporary Chat makes it less traceable, not more acceptable.
rationales: Rewording doesn't make work original or remove IP issues.
Adding sentences doesn't fix the underlying copying.
Correct.
Temporary Chat affects history and training, not IP rights.

questions.stem: You are asked to explain an unfamiliar tax rule to a client. ChatGPT gives a confident, detailed answer you can't evaluate yourself. What should you do?
options: Use it as a first draft, check it against authoritative sources, and have a qualified expert review it before it goes to the client
Send it, since the answer is detailed and confident
Ask ChatGPT whether it is sure, and send it if it says yes
Regenerate until two answers match, then send
questions.explanation: OpenAI advises using ChatGPT as a first draft, not a final source, and confidence isn't reliability. Where you can't judge correctness and the advice may need a licence, involve a qualified professional.
rationales: Correct: verify and get expert review.
Confidence isn't reliability.
Self-assessment by the model isn't verification.
Matching outputs can still both be wrong.

questions.stem: Your team wants ChatGPT to approve or reject small-business loan applications automatically, with no person reviewing the outcome. How does this fit with OpenAI's usage policies?
options: It is fine as long as the prompt tells the model to be fair
It is fine for small amounts
It is prohibited: automating high-stakes decisions in areas such as credit without human review is not allowed
It is fine if the applicants are told afterwards
questions.explanation: The usage policies prohibit automating high-stakes decisions in sensitive areas, including credit, without human review. AI can help structure or summarise, but a person must review the decision.
rationales: A fairness instruction doesn't add human review.
Size doesn't change the high-stakes category.
Correct.
Notification afterwards isn't human review.

questions.stem: You want a patient-facing chatbot built on ChatGPT to give tailored medical advice and introduce itself as "Dr. Assist, your physician". What is the issue?
options: It conflicts with usage policies: tailored advice needing a licence requires a licensed professional involved, and the AI must not imply it holds credentials
None, as long as answers are accurate
Only the name needs to change
It is fine on a workspace plan
questions.explanation: The usage policies prohibit tailored licensed advice without a licensed professional involved and implying the AI holds professional credentials. A plan type doesn't change usage rules.
rationales: Correct.
Accuracy doesn't satisfy the licensed-professional requirement.
Renaming fixes only part of the problem.
Workspace plans change data handling, not usage policy.

questions.stem: On your personal Plus account you don't want your chats used to improve OpenAI's models. What is the most direct control?
options: Archive each chat after you finish
Ask ChatGPT at the start of each chat not to learn from you
Delete your saved memories
Turn off "Improve the model for everyone" in Data Controls
questions.explanation: On personal plans training is on by default and the Data Controls setting turns it off account-wide. Archiving a chat doesn't change it, and memory settings are a separate feature.
rationales: Archiving doesn't change the training setting.
A prompt instruction doesn't change account settings.
Memory is separate from model training.
Correct.
